slides.heading: Design the Uber API
slides.subtitle: SystemsExpert design walkthrough
slides.narration: In this lecture we design the Uber API. We'll follow the interview framework: clarify, set requirements, estimate, sketch the architecture, define the data and API, then dive into the hard parts and the trade-offs.

slides.heading: Clarifying questions
bullets: Rider and driver APIs both?
Payments in scope?
Real-time location updates required?
slides.narration: Start by clarifying the scope with your interviewer. Good questions here are: Rider and driver APIs both? Payments in scope? Real-time location updates required?

slides.heading: Functional requirements
bullets: Rider: request ride, see ETA/driver location, cancel, rate
Driver: go online/offline, accept ride, update location, complete trip
slides.narration: The functional requirements. Rider: request ride, see ETA or driver location, cancel, rate. Driver: go online or offline, accept ride, update location, complete trip.

slides.heading: Non-functional requirements
bullets: Real-time updates (~seconds)
Idempotent state transitions
slides.narration: The non-functional requirements. Real-time updates (about seconds). Idempotent state transitions.

slides.heading: Capacity estimates
bullets: Drivers send location every ~4 s; ~1M active drivers -> ~250k writes/s to the location service
slides.narration: Now some rough capacity estimates, which drive the design. Drivers send location every about 4 s; about 1M active drivers to about 250k writes per s to the location service.

slides.heading: Capacity: worked out
bullets: 1M active drivers, 1 location update / 4 s
1M ÷ 4 = 250k writes/s
Keep only latest position in memory (~100 B)
1M × 100 B = 100 MB → shard by geo cell
slides.narration: Let's actually work the numbers. A million active drivers each send their location every four seconds. That's two hundred fifty thousand location writes a second. We keep only the latest position per driver in memory, about a hundred bytes each. That's only a hundred megabytes total, but the write rate means we shard by geographic cell.

slides.heading: High-level architecture
slides.narration: Here's the high-level architecture. Rider connects to API. Driver connects to API. API connects to Trips: state machine and Location service - geo index and Matching service and Push / websocket gateway. Matching service connects to Location service - geo index.

slides.heading: Request flow: Request a ride
slides.caption: 1. Rider requests a ride
slides.narration: Let's follow a ride request. The rider sends pickup and destination, and gets back a trip in the requested state.

slides.heading: Request flow: Request a ride
slides.caption: 2. API creates the trip
slides.narration: The API creates the trip record, which is a state machine starting at requested.

slides.heading: Request flow: Request a ride
slides.caption: 3. Find nearby drivers
slides.narration: The matching service asks the location service for available drivers near the pickup point.

slides.heading: Request flow: Request a ride
slides.caption: 4. Geo index lookup
slides.narration: The location service, a geo index over recent driver positions, returns the closest candidates.

slides.heading: Request flow: Request a ride
slides.caption: 5. Offer sent to a driver
slides.narration: The best driver gets an offer over a websocket, with a timeout.

slides.heading: Request flow: Request a ride
slides.caption: 6. Driver accepts
slides.narration: When the driver accepts, the trip moves to accepted atomically, and the rider is notified.

slides.heading: Data model
bullets: Trip{tripId, riderId, driverId?, status: REQUESTED|ACCEPTED|ARRIVED|IN_PROGRESS|COMPLETED|CANCELLED, pickup, dropoff, fare}
DriverStatus{driverId, online, location, tripId?}
slides.narration: Here is the data model. Trip tripId, riderId, driverId?, status: REQUESTED ACCEPTED ARRIVED IN PROGRESS COMPLETED CANCELLED, pickup, dropoff, fare. DriverStatus driverId, online, location, tripId?

slides.heading: API
slides.narration: The API. The main endpoints are: POST trips; GET trips by tripId; POST trips by tripId cancel; POST trips by tripId rating; PUT drivers me status; PUT drivers me location; POST trips by tripId accept; POST trips by tripId arrive. Each one is small, resource-oriented and easy to version.

slides.heading: State machine
bullets: Every transition is validated server-side (e.g. accept only from REQUESTED) with optimistic concurrency, so double taps or two drivers accepting resolve deterministically.
slides.narration: Deep dive: State machine. Every transition is validated server-side (for example accept only from REQUESTED) with optimistic concurrency, so double taps or two drivers accepting resolve deterministically.

slides.heading: Location
bullets: Updates go to an in-memory geo index (geohash/S2 cells) sharded by region; matching queries nearby cells.
slides.narration: Deep dive: Location. Updates go to an in-memory geo index (geohash or S2 cells) sharded by region; matching queries nearby cells.

slides.heading: Push vs poll
bullets: Websocket for live location; polling fallback.
slides.narration: Deep dive: Push versus poll. Websocket for live location; polling fallback.

slides.heading: Key decisions
bullets: In-memory geo index → write rate too high for a DB
Trip as a state machine → no double assignment
WebSockets for drivers → low-latency offers
Shard by city / geo cell → locality of matching
slides.narration: Let's pull together the key decisions. In-memory geo index, because write rate too high for a DB. Trip as a state machine, because no double assignment. WebSockets for drivers, because low-latency offers. Shard by city / geo cell, because locality of matching.

slides.heading: Trade-offs & alternatives
bullets: Separate endpoints per transition are explicit and auditable vs a generic PATCH status
In-memory geo index trades durability for speed (locations are ephemeral anyway)
slides.narration: Finally, the key trade-offs. Separate endpoints per transition are explicit and auditable versus a generic PATCH status. In-memory geo index trades durability for speed (locations are ephemeral anyway).

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: Clarify scope, then functional + non-functional needs
Estimate load to size storage and fan-out
Core pieces: Rider, API, Driver, Trips, Location service - geo index
Know your trade-offs and failure modes
slides.narration: To recap the Uber API: we clarified the scope, set functional and non-functional requirements, estimated the load, sketched an architecture built around Rider, API, Driver, Trips, and walked through the deep dives and trade-offs. Practise explaining each decision out loud.
